mcqs.question: In Container With Most Water, why does the standard algorithm always advance the pointer sitting at the shorter wall?
options: Moving the taller wall can only shrink the width while the limiting height stays capped by the same or a shorter wall, so it can never improve the result
The shorter wall is guaranteed to sit closer to the array's center
Moving the shorter wall is guaranteed to increase the area on the very next comparison
It's an arbitrary tie-breaking convention that doesn't affect correctness
mcqs.explanation: Moving the taller wall inward shrinks the width without any chance of raising the limiting (shorter) height, so it can only tie or lose versus the current pair — moving the shorter wall is the only move that could possibly find a taller limiting wall next. It's not a positional or arbitrary choice; it's provably the only move that isn't strictly wasted.

mcqs.question: Given height[left] < height[right], why is moving right instead of left provably unable to produce a better area?
options: Because right is always assumed to be closer to the array's boundary
The new width is strictly smaller, and the area stays capped by height[left] (the smaller of the two current walls) regardless of what value the new right position holds
Because height[left] changes value the moment right is moved
Because the pattern requires left to move before right by convention
mcqs.explanation: Width strictly decreases and the bottleneck height is still height[left], so no matter what the new right wall's height turns out to be, the resulting area is bounded above by the current one — a full proof, not just an empirical pattern. height[left] itself doesn't change, and there's no fixed move ordering.

mcqs.question: In the two-pointer Trapping Rain Water walkthrough, when height[left] < height[right], why can left's trapped water be computed from leftMax alone, without knowing the exact rightMax?
options: Because rightMax is always exactly equal to height[right]

A wall at least as tall as height[right] is guaranteed to exist on the right, and since that's taller than height[left], the right side can't be the limiting boundary for left's water level — so leftMax alone determines it
Because trapped water never depends on anything to the right of the current position
Because water can only accumulate in the left half of any height array
mcqs.explanation: The comparison height[left] < height[right] itself guarantees a wall tall enough on the right that it isn't the bottleneck for left's cell, so the water above left is safely min-bounded by leftMax without needing the precise rightMax value. Nothing restricts water to one half of the array, and rightMax isn't necessarily equal to height[right] itself.

mcqs.question: What's the fundamental difference between the correctness argument for sorted-array two pointers and the greedy two pointers used on height arrays?
options: There is no real difference; both ultimately depend on the array being sorted
Height-array problems don't require a correctness proof since the resulting code is short
Sorted-array correctness comes from a structural guarantee about the data's order; height-array correctness comes from a local exchange argument that must be freshly derived for each new problem
Height-array two pointers always run in O(n²), while sorted-array two pointers always run in O(n)
mcqs.explanation: Sorted two pointers lean on a guarantee baked into the data itself (values are ordered), while height-array problems have no such order and instead need a bespoke proof — like the shorter-wall exchange argument — re-derived per problem. Both patterns run in O(n), and code length says nothing about whether a correctness argument is needed.
